findings.issue: isRemoteDefault assumes a remote name is a single path segment, but git accepts remote names that contain '/'. I checked this in a temp repo: `git remote add team/up <url>` succeeds. So refs/remotes/team/up/main splits into remote "team" and branch "up/main", is not treated as a remote default, and is never passed to the range leg's `--not`.
findings.consequence: For users whose upstream remote name contains a slash, the stale-local-main problem fixed in d994410 comes back: a branch cut from a fresh team/up/main while local main lags pulls merged branches' runs into its range. This over-blocks and never fails open. A precise fix would read the remote names (`git remote`, or the prefixes from for-each-ref) and match refs/remotes/<known-remote>/main|master.

findings.issue: fsm init treats any failure of the `rev-parse --verify` fold check as 'does not resolve' and records the mis-spelled HEAD (for example `Feat`). scope.Load handles the same failure differently: when the exit code is not 1 it returns an unknown scope, which is fail-closed. The two callers of one rule respond differently to the same git failure.
findings.consequence: On a case-insensitive filesystem, a transient rev-parse failure during init (after symbolic-ref and for-each-ref succeeded) would record branch `Feat`. status folds HEAD to `feat`, so the name leg never matches that run. After a rebase the head leaves the range and the run is classified Orphaned, so it silently stops blocking. This is unlikely because it needs a git failure between two successful calls, but it is the one path in the new code that fails open.

findings.issue: fsm init treats any failure of the new `rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<current>` check the same as git's "no" (exit 1): a timeout, a spawn failure or exit 128 just skips the fold. scope.Load does the opposite and leaves the scope unknown when this same check fails with anything other than exit 1 (scope.go `case code(err) != 1: return s`). Everywhere else in init (symbolic-ref, for-each-ref) a git failure goes through gitFailed/ERR_GIT, but this call does not.
findings.consequence: On a case-insensitive filesystem with HEAD spelled `Feat` for branch `feat`, a transient git failure at this call makes init record branch `Feat` without any error. Status later folds Current to `feat`, so the run matches only while its head is in range. After a rebase it is classed as orphaned (no branch `Feat` is listed) and stops blocking. This needs a transient git failure during init together with a mis-cased checkout, so it is not normal usage. The fix is to route `err != nil || code > 1` through gitFailed("rev-parse", ...).

findings.issue: fsm init's new fold check ignores a failed `rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<spelling>`. Any failure (a timeout, or an exit code other than 1) leaves the mis-spelled HEAD unfolded, and init records it (e.g. "Feat") without error. scope.Load does the same check but fails closed: an exit code other than 1 leaves the scope unknown. So the two consumers of the one rule handle a failed check differently, and init differs from its own gitFailed handling of symbolic-ref and for-each-ref failures.
findings.consequence: This needs a case-insensitive filesystem, a mis-cased checkout and a transient git failure during init. The run is then recorded under "Feat", while status on the same checkout folds Current to "feat". The name leg no longer matches, and "Feat" is not a listed branch. Once the branch is rebased and the head leaves the range, the run is classified orphaned and silently stops blocking. The fix is to return gitFailed("rev-parse", code, err) when err != nil or code is neither 0 nor 1.

findings.issue: isRemoteDefault treats the first path segment after refs/remotes/ as the remote name. Git allows remote names that contain a slash (`git remote add team/upstream <url>` yields refs/remotes/team/upstream/main). That remote's default branch is therefore never excluded from the range leg. To tell origin/alice/main apart from a slash-named remote's main, the check needs the configured remote names (`git remote`, or remote.*.fetch).
findings.consequence: This needs a slash-named remote as the only up-to-date copy of main and a stale local main. The stale-main over-block fixed in d994410 then comes back: runs of branches already merged upstream fall into the range of a branch cut from that remote's main, and they block a branch that cannot act on them. The failure blocks too much and never clears a gate.

findings.issue: fsm init treats any failure of the new `rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<current>` check (a timeout, spawn failure, or an exit code other than 1) as "do not fold" and quietly records HEAD's mis-cased spelling. scope.Load handles the same check differently: it folds on success and treats any exit other than 1 as unknown scope (fail closed). Every other git call in init that fails returns ERR_GIT. This one alone swallows the error.
findings.consequence: This needs a case-insensitive filesystem, a mis-cased checkout (`git checkout Feat` for feat) and a transient git failure during init, so it is very unlikely. If it happens, init records branch "Feat", while status later folds Current to "feat". The run then misses the name leg: it is in scope only while its head stays in the range, and after a rebase it reads as orphaned instead of blocking feat. Making this path return gitFailed("rev-parse", code, err) when code != 1 would match Load and the rest of init.

findings.issue: fsm init's new case-fold check handles a failing `rev-parse --verify` differently from scope.Load. Load treats any exit other than 1 as a git failure and leaves the scope unknown (fail closed). init silently skips the fold on any failure (a spawn error, a timeout, exit 128) and records HEAD's mis-spelled name (e.g. "Feat") without raising ERR_GIT. Every other git call in this block goes through gitFailed.
findings.consequence: This needs a transient git failure during init on a case-insensitive checkout where HEAD is spelled differently from the listed branch. Then the run is recorded under a name git never lists. It keeps blocking only through the range leg. After the branch is rebased, status classifies it as orphaned, so the abandoned run stops blocking. The window is narrow, but the handling is inconsistent with the fail-closed rule stated for the branch scope. Treating code != 0 && code != 1 (or err != nil) as gitFailed("rev-parse", ...) would match Load.

findings.issue: Case folding now only happens when `git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<HEAD spelling>` resolves, and that is not a stable sign of a case-insensitive filesystem. The mis-spelled HEAD resolves only while the branch is a loose ref. Once `git gc` or auto-gc runs `pack-refs --all`, the packed-refs lookup is case-sensitive. I checked this on macOS: `checkout -b feat; checkout main; checkout Feat` gives HEAD refs/heads/Feat and rev-parse rc=0. After `git pack-refs --all`, rev-parse gives rc=1. At that point Load keeps Current="Feat", which is not folded, and ForkPoint on the now-unborn HEAD returns no error, so the scope is known with an empty range. Runs that init recorded as "feat" (folded earlier, while the ref was loose) then classify as other-branch. Before ce80bb4 the fold was unconditional and those runs kept blocking.
findings.consequence: On a case-insensitive filesystem, a branch checked out with the wrong case stops being blocked by its own abandoned runs after the next auto-gc packs refs. Git itself shows the checkout as unborn in that state ("No commits yet"), so the breakage is visible and needs an earlier mis-cased checkout. That is why this is advisory. A more stable signal would be `core.ignorecase`, which git sets at init on case-insensitive filesystems, used instead of or alongside the resolve check.

findings.issue: fsm init ignores any failure of the new `rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<current>` check: a timeout, a spawn error or an exit code other than 1 just skips the fold, and init records the HEAD spelling (for example "Feat"). scope.Load treats the same failure as unknown, which fails closed. Later, when status folds the spelling to "feat", it no longer matches the recorded "Feat".
findings.consequence: If git fails transiently during init on a mis-cased checkout, the run is recorded under a spelling no branch has. After a rebase moves its head out of range, the run classifies as orphaned and stops blocking. This needs both a mis-cased HEAD and a transient git failure, so the chance is low. A fix would call gitFailed("rev-parse", ...) when the code is not 1, matching the symbolic-ref and for-each-ref handling above it.

findings.issue: The only test that exercises init's new fold path (rev-parse --verify of the mis-spelled HEAD, then Canonical) and the new canonical --for-branch comparison (`scope.Canonical(branch, branches) != current`, which records `current` on a restatement) skips itself on any case-sensitive filesystem. CI runs on ubuntu-latest, and in a golang:1.26 Linux container it reports SKIP. So CI never runs the run.go lines 302-316 changed in ce80bb4. scope.Load has a fake-git unit test for the same decision (TestLoadFoldsOnlyAResolvingSpelling), but init has none that doesn't depend on the filesystem.
findings.consequence: A regression in init's fold or --for-branch restatement logic (for example comparing the raw branch again, or recording the HEAD spelling) would pass CI and only show up on a macOS developer machine. A mis-cased run name reads as orphaned once its head leaves the range, and then blocks nothing.

findings.issue: init treats every rev-parse outcome except success (err == nil && code == 0) as 'the spelling does not resolve'. That includes a timeout or spawn error (err != nil) and a real git failure (code 128). scope.Load makes the same check fail closed: code != 1 leaves the scope unknown. The two paths now disagree, and no test covers init's failure case (Load's 128 case is tested).

Unlikely, but it's the only fail-open spot in this commit. Returning gitFailed("rev-parse", ...) when code is neither 0 nor 1 would match Load.

verdict.reasoning: The defect is present in the diff. isRemoteDefault splits the remote-tracking suffix at the first slash and accepts only an exact remaining branch name of main or master. Therefore refs/remotes/team/up/main is rejected even though team/up can be a valid remote name. That ref is omitted from rev-list's --not exclusions, so commits already on that remote default branch can incorrectly enter inRange when the local default branch lags, causing unrelated obligations to be classified InScope. The proposed fix direction is appropriate.

The diff only canonicalizes `current` when `rev-parse` returns `err == nil && code == 0`; every other result, including spawn errors, timeouts, and exit codes other than Git's expected not-found code 1, is silently ignored. That can preserve a noncanonical branch spelling the surrounding code explicitly intends to correct, allowing `Branch` to be recorded under a name absent from `branches`. This is inconsistent with the adjacent Git checks and can break later exact branch matching as described. Non-not-found failures should be routed through `gitFailed`.

The diff only canonicalizes `current` when `rev-parse` returns `(err == nil, code == 0)` and silently ignores every other result, including execution errors and unexpected exit codes. It then assigns that unlisted spelling to `branch`, contradicting the stated invariant that the branch is recorded exactly as Git lists it. Since the surrounding Git probes fail on unexpected errors, this unchecked probe can verifiably allow a noncanonical branch value into `machine.Init`; the proposed fail-closed fix is appropriate.

The finding is grounded in isRemoteDefault: after stripping refs/remotes/, it splits only at the first slash and accepts the remainder only when it is exactly main or master. A configured remote named team/upstream produces refs/remotes/team/upstream/main, which is rejected because the parsed branch is upstream/main. That ref is consequently omitted from the rev-list --not exclusions, so commits already present on that remote default branch can incorrectly enter inRange and make unrelated recorded items InScope. This is a concrete conservative over-blocking defect in the stated range behavior.

The diff handles all `rev-parse` failures as if the differently spelled ref simply did not resolve. An execution error or exit code other than Git's expected not-found code 1 therefore leaves `current` non-canonical and still stores it in `InitOptions.Branch`. Because the surrounding Git operations fail closed and exact branch-name matching is explicitly required, this can mis-scope the run and later remove its branch-name blocking path. Unexpected errors and exit codes should return `ERR_GIT`; only exit 1 should preserve the unborn-branch behavior.

The described path follows directly from Load: when Current is not an exact key in branches, Canonical is called only if rev-parse resolves the differently cased ref. If packed-ref lookup returns exit 1, Current remains "Feat" while branches still contains "feat"; with no range match, Classify("feat", ...) reaches the live-branch case and returns OtherBranch. This can clear the current branch's obligations and contradicts the stated case-insensitive canonicalization invariant. The packed-refs reproduction makes the issue concrete rather than speculative.

The diff ignores all non-success outcomes from the canonicalizing rev-parse call, including execution errors and unexpected exit codes, even though adjacent Git operations fail initialization on those conditions. That can leave current in a noncanonical spelling and persist Branch with a value absent from the enumerated local-branch map, undermining the branch ownership invariant this code is intended to enforce. The proposed handling of exit code 1 as a normal missing-ref result and other failures via gitFailed is appropriate.

The added init-specific test for case-folding and canonical --for-branch restatement explicitly skips when refs/heads/MAIN does not resolve, which is the normal behavior on case-sensitive Linux filesystems. The other added tests exercise exact branch names and therefore would not fail if init regressed to comparing or recording the raw mis-cased spelling. The stated repository search found only scope.Load's analogous fake-git test, not a platform-independent init test, so the new init invariant is not enforced in Linux CI. Under the review criteria, this working-but-unpinned invariant is a real pre-merge defect.

The diff explicitly intends to canonicalize a differently cased symbolic-ref against the branch names returned by for-each-ref, but the rev-parse probe silently ignores every non-success result. Code 1 can legitimately mean the spelling does not resolve; an execution error or another Git exit code means canonicalization could not be determined and should fail closed, as the preceding Git probes do. Continuing can persist a noncanonical branch name that exact status matching will not recognize after commit reachability changes. The shown tests exercise a code-128 path in scope classification, but no displayed init test pins this rev-parse failure behavior.

The diff only canonicalizes `current` when `rev-parse` returns `err == nil && code == 0`; every other result, including execution errors and unexpected exit codes, is silently ignored. Execution then records the uncanonicalized symbolic-ref spelling in `Branch`. Given the surrounding comments explicitly require Git-listed canonical spelling so status matching cannot orphan a run, allowing operational Git failures to bypass canonicalization violates that fail-closed invariant. Unexpected errors/codes should produce `ERR_GIT`, while exit 1 may legitimately mean the ref did not resolve.

The diff only canonicalizes a mis-cased current branch when `rev-parse` returns `(err == nil, code == 0)` and silently treats every other result as “do not fold.” Thus an execution error or unexpected exit leaves `current` in a spelling absent from `branches`, after which that spelling is unconditionally stored in `Branch`. This violates the diff’s own exact-name invariant and differs from the surrounding git probes, which fail with ERR_GIT. The narrow failure conditions make it uncommon, but the fail-open path is concrete and should distinguish the expected negative result from actual git failures.

The stale-main over-block fixed in d994410 then comes back: runs of branches already merged upstream fall into the range of a branch cut from that remote's main, and they block a branch that cannot act on them. The failure blocks too much and never clears a gate.

[ADVISORY] fsm init's new case-fold check handles a failing `rev-parse --verify` differently from scope.Load. Load treats any exit other than 1 as a git failure and leaves the scope unknown (fail closed). init silently skips the fold on any failure (a spawn error, a timeout, exit 128) and records HEAD's mis-spelled name (e.g. "Feat") without raising ERR_GIT. Every other git call in this block goes through gitFailed. This needs a transient git failure during init on a case-insensitive checkout where HEAD is spelled differently from the listed branch. Then the run is recorded under a name git never lists. It keeps blocking only through the range leg. After the branch is rebased, status classifies it as orphaned, so the abandoned run stops blocking. The window is narrow, but the handling is inconsistent with the fail-closed rule stated for the branch scope. [ADVISORY] Case folding now only happens when `git rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<HEAD spelling>` resolves, and that is not a stable sign of a case-insensitive filesystem. The mis-spelled HEAD resolves only while the branch is a loose ref. Once `git gc` or auto-gc runs `pack-refs --all`, the packed-refs lookup is case-sensitive. I checked this on macOS: `checkout -b feat; checkout main; checkout Feat` gives HEAD refs/heads/Feat and rev-parse rc=0. After `git pack-refs --all`, rev-parse gives rc=1. At that point Load keeps Current="Feat", which is not folded, and ForkPoint on the now-unborn HEAD returns no error, so the scope is known with an empty range. Runs that init recorded as "feat" (folded earlier, while the ref was loose) then classify as other-branch. Before ce80bb4 the fold was unconditional and those runs kept blocking. On a case-insensitive filesystem, a branch checked out with the wrong case stops being blocked by its own abandoned runs after the next auto-gc packs refs. Git itself shows the checkout as unborn in that state ("No commits yet"), so the breakage is visible and needs an earlier mis-cased checkout. That is why this is advisory. A more stable signal would be `core.ignorecase`, which git sets at init on case-insensitive filesystems, used instead of or alongside the resolve check.
